subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
Parul: They did it AGAIN. Dad told the relatives I'm doing an MBA. I never said that 😠
Harish: Whoa. What did you say when he said it?
Parul: Nothing. I walked out and slammed my door.
Harish: Fair, honestly. Are you going to yell at dinner?
Parul: I want to. I really want to.
Harish: Maybe wait till tomorrow? Write down what you actually want and one example.
Parul: Ugh. Fine. Example: Sunday, he filled in my college form without asking me.
Harish: That's a good one. Say that, not "you never listen".
Parul: ...okay. Tomorrow after chai. Thanks for not telling me to calm down 🙂

qa.q: What did Dad tell the relatives about Parul?
qa.a: That Parul is doing an MBA.

qa.q: How is Parul feeling, and what does Parul do with the feeling?
qa.a: Furious and unheard. Parul walked out, slammed the door and admits really wanting to yell at dinner.

qa.q: What advice from Harish helps most?
qa.a: To wait until tomorrow and write down what Parul wants along with a concrete example, such as the college form, rather than saying "you never listen".

qa.q: How might Parul's father see the situation?
qa.a: He may think he is helping and not realise Parul feels ignored. A specific example is easier for him to hear than a general complaint.

grounding: Parul is furious that the parents ignore what Parul wants; Parul lets the anger cool and prepares to say what Parul needs calmly with examples.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
Monday: Rekha's parents told her at dinner that they had already paid the deposit for MBA coaching in Chandigarh. She had told them twice she wanted to do the fine-arts master's. She shouted, "You never listen!" and slammed her door so hard the calendar fell.
Tuesday: She didn't speak to them all day. At college she vented to Baljeet in the canteen. He let her finish, then asked, "Do you want to win the fight or get them to understand?" She walked around the campus lake twice before she had an answer.
Thursday: After dinner she sat with them, calmer. "When you paid without asking me, I felt invisible. In March I showed you my portfolio, and in June I told you about the art master's. Both times the topic changed. I need you to hear me this time." Her mother looked at her father. "We thought it was a phase," he said. "Show us the portfolio again."

qa.q: How did Rekha feel on Monday when she heard about the deposit?
qa.a: Furious and unheard, so she shouted and slammed her door.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Thursday?
qa.a: Rekha let the anger cool, talked it through with Baljeet, then spoke calmly with specific examples from March and June and a clear need.

qa.q: How had Rekha's parents seen her wish for the art master's?
qa.a: As a phase; after her calm examples, they asked to see the portfolio again.

grounding: Shows fury at parents ignoring one's wishes, letting the anger cool and then stating needs calmly with examples.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
Ganga, beti, you're angry with your parents? Sit. Your Vijay Dada has a story about anger.
In 1974 I was twenty-one, in Jhansi. I wanted to join the Railways as a mechanic. My father wanted me in his cloth shop. He wouldn't even let me finish a sentence about it.
So I did the dramatic thing. I packed a tin trunk and told him, "If you won't listen, I'm leaving for Bombay tomorrow." He said, "Go, then." And I went, all the way to the bus stand, and sat there till midnight, too proud to go back and too scared to leave.
Your Dadi, only a neighbour then, found me and said, "Threats won't make him hear you."
A week later, calm, I sat beside him in the shop and said, "Babuji, I love you. I'm not good with cloth. I'm good with engines. Let me try for one year." He was quiet a long time. Then he said, "One year."
Anger is a messenger, beti. Let it deliver the message, then send it home.

qa.q: Where did young Vijay sit till midnight?
How did Vijay feel sitting at the bus stand?
qa.a: Torn and stuck: too proud to go back and too scared to leave after his angry threat.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vijay's story?
qa.a: The neighbour who later became Ganga's Dadi telling him threats wouldn't work; a week later he spoke calmly and asked for a one-year trial.

qa.q: How might Vijay's father have felt when Vijay packed the trunk?
qa.a: Hurt and defensive, answering "Go, then" out of pride.

grounding: Illustrates anger at a parent who will not listen, the failure of dramatic threats, and the calm request that finally gets heard.
